items.label: section_header
items.text: CHANGING THE TEMPERATURE

items.label: section_header
items.text: REMINDER

items.label: text
items.text: Exothermic and endothermic reactions and ∆H values are explained in Chapter 19.

items.label: list_item
items.text: Figure 21.7 If a reaction is exothermic in the forward reaction it will be endothermic in the reverse direction.

items.label: section_header
items.text: KEY POINT

items.label: text
items.text: At equilibrium, the rate of the forward reaction is equal to the rate of the reverse reaction so as much heat is being given out as is taken in – nothing appears to change.

items.label: section_header
items.text: KEY POINT

items.label: text
items.text: In an endothermic reaction the heat is converted to a different form (chemical energy), so it is being removed.

items.label: text
items.text: If you increase the pressure, the reaction will respond by reducing it again. It can reduce the pressure by producing fewer gaseous molecules to hit the walls of the container, in this case by converting A + 2B (3 molecules) into C + D (2 molecules). Increasing the pressure will always cause the position of equilibrium to shift in the direction which produces the smaller number of gaseous molecules.

items.label: text
items.text: Consider the reaction between nitrogen gas and hydrogen gas to make ammonia:

items.label: formula
items.text: N _ { 2 } ( g ) + 3 H _ { 2 } ( g ) \rightleftharpoons 2 N H _ { 3 } ( g )

items.label: text
items.text: If we want to make as much ammonia as possible, we need to make the pressure as high as possible. There are four molecules of gas on the left-hand side but only two on the right-hand side. Increasing the pressure will therefore shift the position of equilibrium to the right (the ammonia side), the side with fewer gas molecules.

items.label: text
items.text: If there is the same number of gaseous molecules on both sides of the equation, changing the pressure will make no difference to the position of equilibrium. For example, in this reaction:

items.label: formula
items.text: H _ { 2 } ( g ) + I _ { 2 } ( g ) \rightleftharpoons 2 H I ( g )

items.label: text
items.text: increasing or decreasing the pressure has no effect on the position of equ           ugen iodide we have at equilibrium.

items.label: section_header
items.text: To summarise:

items.label: text
items.text: Increasing pressure: the position of equilibrium shifts to the side which has fewer gas molecules.

items.label: text
items.text: Decreasing pressure: the position of equilibrium shifts to the side which has more gas molecules.

items.label: text
items.text: When we write a reversible reaction showing an enthalpy change, the ∆H always shows the enthalpy change for the forward reaction. The value of ∆H is given as if the reaction was a one-way process.

items.label: formula
items.text: A + 2 B \rightleftharpoons C + D \quad \Delta H = - 1 0 0 k J / m o l

items.label: text
items.text: So, in this case ∆H being negative tells us that the forward reaction is exothermic.

items.label: text
items.text: The reverse reaction will be endothermic by exactly the same amount.

items.label: text
items.text: Suppose you changed the conditions by decreasing the temperature of the equilibrium, for example if the reaction was originally in equilibrium at 500 °C you lower the temperature to 100 °C. The reaction will respond in a way that increases the temperature again. How can it do that?

items.label: text
items.text: If some A and B are converted into C and D, more heat is given out because this is an exothermic change. The extra heat that is produced will warm the reaction mixture up again. In other words, decreasing the temperature will cause the position of equilibrium to move to the right-hand side and more C and D to be formed.

items.label: formula
items.text: A + 2 B \rightleftharpoons C + D

items.label: text
items.text: Equilibrium at 500°C 80% 20%

items.label: text
items.text: Equilibrium at 100°C 60% 40%

items.label: text
items.text: Increasing the temperature will have exactly the opposite effect. The reaction equilibrium will change to remove the extra heat by absorbing it in an endothermic change. This time the reverse reaction is favoured and the position of equilibrium moves to the left.
